outputs.L3:
The system is designed to predict the value of an unknown attribute with a high degree of accuracy. To achieve this, it uses a co-clustering approach that analyzes relationships between two types of identifiers: first IDs and second IDs.

First, the system performs co-clustering on the first IDs and the second IDs. This process uses first master data associated with the first IDs, second master data associated with the second IDs, and fact data that indicates relationships or interactions between the first IDs and the second IDs. By considering both the attribute information in the master data and the relational information in the fact data, the system can identify meaningful clusters that reflect patterns shared across the two types of IDs.

After the co-clustering process is completed, the system generates a prediction model for each cluster of first IDs. Each prediction model is trained to capture the characteristics and tendencies of the first IDs belonging to the corresponding cluster. As a result, the system can provide more specialized and accurate predictions than a single general-purpose model.

When a user specifies a particular first ID and an objective variable to be predicted, the system estimates the value of that objective variable for the specified first ID. In making this prediction, the system does not rely solely on one cluster or one model. Instead, it uses both the prediction models generated for the respective clusters and the probability that the specified first ID belongs to each cluster.

More specifically, the system calculates or references the membership probability of the first ID for each cluster, applies the prediction model associated with each cluster, and combines the resulting predictions according to those probabilities. This enables the system to reflect uncertainty in cluster membership and produce a final predicted value that is weighted by the likelihood of the first ID belonging to each cluster.

Through this method, the system can accurately predict an unknown attribute value by integrating master data, relationship data, cluster-specific prediction models, and probabilistic cluster membership information.
outputs.L4:
A prediction system is provided for estimating unknown attribute values associated with an ID, such as a user, customer, product, facility, account, or other identifiable entity. The system uses two master datasets, each containing a set of IDs and corresponding known attribute information, together with relational fact data that represents relationships, interactions, transactions, events, or links between IDs included in the two master datasets. Examples of such fact data may include purchase histories, access logs, communication records, co-occurrence data, transaction records, or any other data indicating a relationship between entities in the two datasets.

The system first analyzes the relational fact data and performs co-clustering on the IDs contained in the two master datasets. Through this co-clustering process, IDs that exhibit similar relational patterns are grouped together, and clusters are formed in a manner that reflects the structure of relationships between the two datasets. In some cases, each ID may belong to one cluster definitively; in other cases, an ID may have a probability of belonging to each of a plurality of clusters. These belonging probabilities allow the system to represent uncertain or overlapping membership and to capture more detailed relational characteristics than a simple single-cluster assignment.

After the clusters have been generated, the system creates a prediction model for each cluster. Each cluster-specific prediction model is trained using known attribute values and the corresponding data associated with IDs included in, or probabilistically assigned to, that cluster. The prediction models may be generated using various statistical or machine-learning techniques, such as regression analysis, classification methods, decision trees, ensemble learning, matrix factorization, neural networks, or other predictive modeling approaches. Because each model is trained on a cluster having similar relational characteristics, the model can learn patterns that are more specific to that group than a single global model trained on all IDs.

When prediction is to be performed, a target ID and an objective variable are specified. The objective variable represents the attribute value to be predicted, such as a demographic attribute, preference value, risk score, demand amount, likelihood of purchase, category label, numerical measurement, or other unknown or missing attribute. The system identifies the cluster membership information for the target ID, including the probability that the target ID belongs to each cluster. The target ID’s relevant explanatory variables or associated data are then input into the prediction models corresponding to the clusters.

Each cluster-specific model outputs a predicted value for the objective variable. The system then combines these predicted values using the target ID’s belonging probabilities. For example, the final prediction may be calculated as a weighted sum or weighted average of the outputs of the cluster-specific models, where each weight corresponds to the target ID’s probability of belonging to the associated cluster. In this way, the final predicted value reflects both the specialized knowledge learned within each cluster and the degree to which the target ID is associated with that cluster.

By using co-clustering based on relational fact data and by generating prediction models tailored to the resulting clusters, the system can capture hidden structures and dependencies between the two master datasets. This approach enables more accurate prediction of unknown attribute values than methods that rely only on attributes within a single master dataset or that use a single prediction model for all IDs. The use of belonging probabilities further improves prediction accuracy by allowing the system to account for ambiguous or mixed cluster membership rather than forcing each ID into only one group. As a result, the system can provide high-accuracy attribute prediction for target IDs even when direct attribute information is incomplete, sparse, or unavailable.

**The Importance of IDs in a Data-Based World**

The modern digital world is based on information. Every day, people, companies, and organizations use data to make decisions, improve services, and keep systems organized. One important part of this data-based environment is the use of IDs.

IDs help identify people, products, accounts, devices, and records. The purpose of an ID is to make sure that each item or user can be recognized accurately. For example, a customer ID helps a company find the correct account, while a product ID helps track inventory and sales.

The use of IDs also improves security. In many systems, IDs are used together with passwords or other verification methods to protect personal information. This makes it easier to manage access and reduce mistakes.

Because so many services are based on digital records, IDs have become essential. The ability to organize, search, and protect information depends on clear identification. As technology continues to grow, IDs will remain a key part of how people and systems connect.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract for a system that predicts missing attribute values using co-clustering of IDs from two master data tables and fact data linking them.
counterfactuals.output: A computer-implemented system and method are provided for predicting missing attribute values in master data records. The system receives a first master data table comprising first entity identifiers and associated attributes, a second master data table comprising second entity identifiers and associated attributes, and fact data comprising observed associations between the first entity identifiers and the second entity identifiers. A co-clustering module generates clusters of the first entity identifiers and clusters of the second entity identifiers based on the association structure represented in the fact data, thereby identifying latent relationships between the two entity domains. An attribute inference module uses the generated co-clusters, together with known attribute values in one or both master data tables, to estimate one or more missing attribute values for a target record. The estimation may be based on attribute distributions, similarity measures, cluster membership probabilities, or combinations thereof. The predicted attribute values are output for storage, display, validation, or automated enrichment of the master data tables. The system enables completion of incomplete master data by leveraging relational patterns in linked transactional or fact data rather than relying solely on direct attribute similarity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the invention in formal patent language: first master data, second master data, fact data relating first IDs and second IDs, co-clustering means, prediction model generation means, and prediction means.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention relates to an information processing system, method, and program for generating predictions by using relational data between different types of master data.

The invention comprises: first master data including a plurality of first records respectively identified by first identifiers; second master data including a plurality of second records respectively identified by second identifiers; and fact data including relation records in which the first identifiers and the second identifiers are associated with one another. Co-clustering means performs co-clustering on the basis of the fact data so as to classify the first identifiers into first clusters and the second identifiers into second clusters while taking into account relationships between the first identifiers and the second identifiers. Prediction model generation means generates a prediction model using, as explanatory information, cluster information obtained by the co-clustering means and information contained in at least one of the first master data, the second master data, and the fact data. Prediction means applies the generated prediction model to target data including at least one of a first identifier and a second identifier, or information associated therewith, thereby predicting a value, class, probability, score, recommendation, or other target information relating to a relationship between the first master data and the second master data.

According to the invention, hidden relational structures between two different data domains can be extracted from fact data and incorporated into a prediction model, thereby improving prediction accuracy even when individual master data alone is insufficient to represent interactions between the first identifiers and the second identifiers.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an abstract for an AI/data mining apparatus that predicts an unknown attribute of a record using co-clustering, cluster-specific models, and belonging probabilities.
counterfactuals.output: An artificial intelligence and data mining apparatus is configured to predict an unknown attribute of a data record by using co-clustering and cluster-specific predictive models. The apparatus includes one or more processors and memory storing instructions that cause the apparatus to receive a dataset comprising a plurality of records and attributes, perform co-clustering on the dataset to identify clusters of records and corresponding clusters of attributes, and generate, for each identified cluster, a predictive model trained using data associated with that cluster. For a target record having an unknown attribute value, the apparatus determines belonging probabilities indicating a degree to which the target record belongs to respective record clusters and/or attribute clusters. The apparatus applies one or more cluster-specific predictive models to the target record and combines outputs of the models according to the belonging probabilities to generate a predicted value for the unknown attribute. The apparatus may iteratively update the co-clusters, belonging probabilities, and predictive models as additional records are received, thereby improving prediction accuracy for sparse, high-dimensional, or partially observed datasets.

counterfactuals.prompt: Convert the following concept into a Japanese patent-style English abstract: co-cluster first and second IDs from relational fact data, build prediction models per first-ID cluster, and predict an objective variable for a specified first ID.
counterfactuals.output:
PROBLEM TO BE SOLVED: To improve prediction accuracy for an objective variable associated with a specified first ID by utilizing relational fact data including first IDs and second IDs.

SOLUTION: An information processing apparatus acquires relational fact data representing relationships between a plurality of first IDs and a plurality of second IDs. The apparatus performs co-clustering on the first IDs and the second IDs based on the relational fact data, thereby generating one or more first-ID clusters and one or more second-ID clusters. For each of the first-ID clusters, the apparatus constructs a prediction model for predicting an objective variable, using data corresponding to first IDs included in the relevant first-ID cluster. When a specified first ID is received, the apparatus identifies a first-ID cluster to which the specified first ID belongs, selects the prediction model corresponding to the identified first-ID cluster, and predicts the objective variable for the specified first ID by using the selected prediction model. Accordingly, a prediction model adapted to characteristics of a cluster obtained from relational structure can be used, thereby enabling highly accurate prediction even when the relational fact data is sparse or heterogeneous.
